 Early Sunday morning marked the ending of Daylight Savings time. It’s a topic that’s been widely debated in Florida's state legislature. (Spectrum News/Maggie Rickerby) 
 Clocks fall back an hour after Senate stalls proposed permanent time bill
 BY 
 Maggie Rickerby
 Florida 
 PUBLISHED 4:53 PM ET Nov. 01, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 4:53 PM EST Nov. 01, 2026 
 SHARE 
 FLORIDA — Nov. 1 marks the end of Daylight Saving Time in 2026.
 The clocks fall back an hour, despite national and statewide efforts to establish daylight saving time year round.
 In July of this year, U.S. Congress passed the Sunshine Protection Act in the House of Representatives, but when it came to the Senate, the proposed bill stalled.
 The bipartisan backed bill was introduced by Florida Sen. Rick Scott. It would make daylight saving time permanent. That means, if passed, Americans would no longer fall back an hour in November.
 Supporters, like President Donald Trump and Scott, say the extra sunlight at the end of the day would be a good thing. They also say people are tired of changing their clocks.
 In a recent post on X, Scott said: “Tonight, we once again have to take part in the outdated practice of changing our clocks. Americans are tired of it. It’s time for the Senate to pass my Sunshine Protection Act to get rid of this ridiculous time change.”
 Bernita Wells in Orlando said that while it’s not her decision to make, here in Florida, it’s in the name.
 “For me personally, (we're) in the Sunshine State you know, bring on the sunshine,” Wells said.
 Sen. Tom Cotton in Arkansas has been outspoken about his opposition to the proposed bill. He said he worries dark mornings could be a safety hazard for children at school bus stops and people working early in the morning.
 Jenny Nguyen said she’s mostly indifferent on the issue because her kids are now in college. But she sees another perspective.
 “If you have little kids, absolutely — I mean, I can see why they are thinking about that,” Nguyen said.
 Dorcas Dillard said she’s fine sticking with the status quo.
 “Because we’re already on that system so, I like it the way it is. So every time, fall back, go forward, so I like it,” Dillard said.
 According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, Florida is among 19 states that have enacted legislation to keep daylight saving time year round.
 But, federal laws don’t allow them to go into effect. The federal Uniform Time Act says that states can implement standard time year-round, but they can’t implement daylight savings year-round.
 As it stands, the national Sunshine Protection Act has not gone into place and clocks have officially fallen back.
